common_name: Callosum Slipper Orchid (Painted-Lip Paphiopedilum, Mottled-Leaf Lady Slipper)

planting.note: Divide and repot multi-growth clumps in spring into a fine, fast-draining terrestrial orchid mix (small fir bark, perlite, and sphagnum moss) in a shallow pot sized just larger than the root mass; Paphiopedilum callosum has no water-storing pseudobulbs, so newly divided fans should never be allowed to dry out completely while re-establishing.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light equivalent to an east window or a spot several feet back from a south window — direct sun scorches the foliage, while too little light prevents blooming. Paphiopedilum callosum is a terrestrial and lithophytic slipper orchid from Thailand, Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam, prized for its handsome tessellated foliage (dark green mottled with lighter gray-green) and for producing a single, long-lasting flower per stem: a broad white-and-maroon-veined dorsal sepal above twisted, hair-fringed petals and a purple-brown pouch. Because it lacks pseudobulbs, the fine bark-and-sphagnum mix should stay evenly moist year-round with no dry rest period, though the pot must drain freely to avoid crown rot. This species is the principal parent of the mottled-leaf "Maudiae-type" hybrids that dominate garden-center slipper orchid displays, making it one of the most horticulturally influential species in the genus.

common_name: Showy Pansy Orchid (Brazilian Miltonia, Spectabilis Orchid)

planting.note: Divide clumps of 3+ pseudobulbs in spring just as new growth emerges and pot in a fine bark-and-sphagnum mix in a shallow, well-drained container; Miltonia spectabilis is a warm-growing Brazilian lowland species and, unlike its cooler-growing relative Miltoniopsis, tolerates typical indoor room warmth without complaint.

directions: Provide bright, filtered light — an east or lightly shaded south window — with high humidity and good air movement around the flattened, oval pseudobulbs. Miltonia spectabilis is an epiphytic orchid from the Atlantic coastal forests of Brazil, producing broad, flat, pansy-shaped flowers 2–3 inches across in late summer and fall: white to rose-pink sepals and petals surround a large, flaring lip that is white with a bold purple-red blotch radiating from its base. Keep the bark mix evenly moist through the growing season and reduce watering only slightly after flowering, since this species has no pronounced dry dormancy and resents prolonged drying at the roots. It is one of the classic "pansy orchids" of the trade and considerably easier in average home warmth than the similarly named but cooler-growing Miltoniopsis hybrids.

common_name: Cool-Growing Pansy Orchid (Colombian Miltoniopsis, Vexillaria Orchid)

planting.note: Repot annually or every other year into fresh, fine-grade bark-and-sphagnum mix, since this species is highly sensitive to salt buildup and stale, decomposing media; Miltoniopsis vexillaria is a cloud-forest native of Colombia and Ecuador that performs best where summer temperatures stay below the mid-80s°F, making it better suited to bright windowsills or cooled greenhouses than hot, humid porches.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light and cool-to-intermediate temperatures with consistent moisture — the thin, soft, light-green leaves pleat or crease visibly when watering is inconsistent, giving growers a reliable early warning sign of stress. Miltoniopsis vexillaria produces flat, rounded, fragrant flowers 2–3 inches across in white, pink, magenta, or red, most with a contrasting darker "mask" or waterfall pattern radiating from the center of the lip, typically blooming in spring on upright spikes of 4–6 flowers. Water thoroughly whenever the fine bark mix approaches dryness at the surface, and flush the pot regularly with plain water to prevent the fertilizer salt buildup that quickly browns the sensitive leaf tips. This is the cool-growing "pansy orchid" most often sold alongside Phalaenopsis in supermarket and garden-center orchid displays, and it is a parent of the majority of hybrid Miltoniopsis sold commercially.

common_name: Blue Vanda (Autumn Vanda, Tessellated Blue Orchid)

planting.note: Mount on a slab or hang bare-root in a slatted teak basket with little or no medium so the thick silver aerial roots have maximum air exposure; Vanda coerulea comes from cooler mid-elevation hills of Assam, Myanmar, and Thailand with a distinct cool, dry winter, and is more temperature-tolerant than most Vandas but still needs very bright light and daily root wetting followed by rapid drying to thrive. Source only nursery-propagated plants, as wild collection helped make this species one of the first orchids protected under international trade law.

directions: Provide very bright light — more than most Phalaenopsis or Cattleya tolerate — with strong air movement around the roots, since Vanda coerulea is a monopodial, leafless-root epiphyte that depends on frequent wetting and thorough drying rather than a bark potting mix. This is the famous "Blue Vanda" of the Khasi Hills, historically significant as one of the first orchids to display true blue-violet pigment, with a distinctive checkered (tessellated) pattern across the 4-inch flowers borne on upright racemes in fall. Water or mist the aerial roots daily in warm weather and let them dry within a few hours; humidity should stay high but standing moisture on the roots invites rot. Vanda coerulea is the parent species behind the great majority of blue-flowered Vanda hybrids in cultivation today, including the classic Vanda 'Rothschildiana.'
sources: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species

common_name: Walker's Cattleya (Miniature Cattleya, Compact Walkeriana Orchid)

planting.note: Mount small divisions on a cork or tree-fern slab, or pot loosely in coarse bark in a small clay pot, so roots dry quickly between waterings; Cattleya walkeriana is a compact, rock- and tree-dwelling Brazilian species that stays under 8 inches tall, making it one of the few full-sized-flowered Cattleyas suited to a bright windowsill rather than a greenhouse bench.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light similar to other Cattleyas — a lightly shaded south or unobstructed east window — and allow the small pseudobulbs to dry noticeably between waterings. Cattleya walkeriana, native to rocky outcrops and tree branches in Minas Gerais and Goiás, Brazil, is unusual among Cattleyas for its miniature stature paired with large, intensely fragrant, 3–4-inch lavender-pink to white flowers that open from the base of a new growth before or as the single leaf fully expands. Give a brief, cooler, drier rest in late winter after growths mature to encourage the following season's flower buds, then resume regular watering as new roots appear in spring. Its compact size and outsized, fragrant blooms have made it one of the most sought-after species for breeding smaller, windowsill-friendly Cattleya hybrids.

common_name: Pink Rock Orchid (Kingianum Orchid, Australian Rock Orchid)

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in spring after flowering and pot in a fast-draining bark-and-perlite mix in a shallow container; Dendrobium kingianum is a lithophytic species from rocky outcrops in eastern Australia and is among the most cold-tolerant orchids grown, surviving brief drops to near freezing when kept dry, so it can summer outdoors in a bright spot in most temperate climates.

directions: Grow in bright light with some direct morning sun — more light than a typical Phalaenopsis needs — and let the compact, clustering canes dry between waterings. Dendrobium kingianum forms tight clumps of short, tapering, cane-like pseudobulbs and is one of the easiest and most reliably floriferous orchids for beginners, producing clusters of small, fragrant, white-to-deep-pink flowers at the cane tips in late winter and spring. A distinct, cool, dry rest from late fall into winter, with night temperatures allowed to drop into the 40s°F, is essential for heavy flowering and also toughens the plant against occasional cold snaps. Because it tolerates more cold and neglect than most orchids, it is widely sold as a beginner-friendly "rock orchid" and adapts well to being grown outdoors on a porch or patio for much of the year in mild climates.

common_name: Silver-Leaf Moth Orchid (Schiller's Phalaenopsis, Rose Moth Orchid)

planting.note: Pot offsets (keikis) or divisions in a coarse bark-and-sphagnum mix in a clear or slatted container that lets light reach the roots; Phalaenopsis schilleriana is a warm, low-light-tolerant Philippine species best grown at typical indoor room temperature away from direct sun, at an east window or a few feet back from a bright south or west window.

directions: Grow in bright, indirect light — direct sun quickly scorches the broad leaves — and water thoroughly, then allow the bark mix to approach dryness before watering again. Phalaenopsis schilleriana is prized for foliage nearly as ornamental as its flowers: broad, strap-shaped leaves marbled in silvery gray over dark green, arising in a fanned rosette with no pseudobulbs to store water. In winter and spring, a long, branched, arching inflorescence carries dozens of soft rose-pink flowers over many weeks, and the spike can be cut back to a lower node after bloom to sometimes trigger a second flush. This species is one of the principal ancestors of the mottled-leaf, pink-flowered Phalaenopsis hybrids sold everywhere as houseplants, and it shares the same easy, low-light, no-rest-period culture as its relatives.

planting.note: Mount on a slab or pot loosely in a small amount of coarse bark in a small pot, since Psychopsis papilio dislikes having its roots disturbed and produces a single, persistent flower spike that should never be cut off after blooming — it continues to branch and re-flower from the same spike for years.

directions: Grow in bright, filtered light similar to a Cattleya, with warm, humid, well-ventilated conditions and consistent moisture that never becomes stagnant around the single, flattened pseudobulb. Native to Trinidad, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador, and Peru, Psychopsis papilio produces one striking flower at a time atop a tall, wiry, continuously elongating spike — long, twisting, mahogany-and-yellow sepals and petals held above a smaller lip create an uncanny resemblance to a butterfly or moth in flight, a display that can recur intermittently for years from the same spike. The mottled, purplish-green, paddle-shaped leaf is also distinctive and ornamental in its own right. Keep the bark or moss mix lightly moist at all times and avoid letting the roots dry out completely, since this species lacks the substantial water-storing pseudobulbs of many other epiphytic orchids.

planting.note: Hang bare-root in a slatted teak or wire basket with little to no medium so the thick aerial roots dry quickly after watering; Vanda sanderiana is a lowland Philippine species that needs very bright light, warm year-round temperatures, and high humidity, and it is now rare in the wild, so only nursery-propagated stock should be acquired.

directions: Provide very bright light and strong air movement around the exposed roots, watering or misting the root mass thoroughly once or twice daily in warm weather and allowing it to dry within a few hours to prevent rot. Known as Waling-Waling and closely associated with Davao in the southern Philippines, Vanda sanderiana bears some of the largest, flattest flowers in the genus — 4 to 6 inches across, with the upper half of the flower rose-pink and the lower half warm tawny-brown overlaid with fine reddish tessellation. Established, well-grown plants can flower more than once a year given consistently warm temperatures and high humidity. This species has been extensively used in hybridizing large-flowered, brightly patterned Vanda and Ascocenda hybrids and remains one of the most historically important species in Vanda breeding.
sources: IUCN Red List of Threatened Species
